items.q: Which is the ITIL definition of an organization?
o: A group of people working in the same building
A legal entity that is registered to trade
A person or a group of people that has its own functions with responsibilities, authorities and relationships to achieve its objectives
Any group of IT specialists who deliver services
items.x: In ITIL, an organization can be a single person or a large, complex structure, provided it has its own functions, responsibilities, authorities and relationships to achieve its objectives.

items.q: Which statement about value is CORRECT?
o: Value is co-created through active collaboration between providers, consumers and other stakeholders
Value is created by the service provider alone and delivered to a passive consumer
Value is always measured in financial terms
Value is the same for every stakeholder of a service
items.x: Value is perceived and subjective, is not only financial, and is co-created when providers and consumers both contribute, for example consumers defining requirements, using the product correctly and giving feedback.

items.q: A service offering for managed printers includes replacing broken printers within one day. What type of component is the replacement?
o: Goods
Access to resources
Utility
Service action
items.x: Service actions are activities that the provider performs to address a consumer's needs, such as repairs, replacements and user support.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of service CONSUMPTION?
o: The provider monitoring its servers
The consumer managing its own network connection so that users can reach the service
The provider improving service performance
The provider fulfilling an agreed service action
items.x: Service consumption includes the consumer managing the resources it needs to use the service, users performing service actions such as requests, and receiving goods. Options A, C and D are service provision.

items.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
An [?] is a result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs.
o: output
asset
outcome
objective
items.x: An outcome is a result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs. Outputs are the tangible or intangible deliverables of activities.

items.q: What is a risk?
o: A possible event that could cause harm or loss, or make it more difficult to achieve objectives
A known error that has not been resolved
An incident that has a major impact
The cost of a service that is imposed on the consumer
items.x: A risk is a possible event that could cause harm or loss, or make objectives harder to achieve. It can also be defined as uncertainty of outcome, which includes positive outcomes.

items.q: How can a service consumer help reduce the risks of a service it uses?
o: By transferring all risks to the provider through the contract
By actively participating in defining requirements and clearly communicating its critical success factors and constraints
By refusing to share information about its business
By paying a higher price for the service
items.x: Because value is co-created, consumers also contribute to risk reduction. They take part in defining requirements and clarifying outcomes, communicate critical success factors and constraints, and give the provider access to the resources it needs.

items.q: Which term describes a product or service that is 'fit for purpose'?
o: Warranty
Sustainability
Availability
Utility
items.x: Utility, or fitness for purpose, is the functionality that meets a need. Warranty, or fitness for use, is the assurance that agreed requirements such as availability, capacity, security and continuity will be met.

items.q: What is a change?
o: A request from a user for information
An unplanned interruption to a service
The addition, modification or removal of anything that could have a direct or indirect effect on services
The replacement of a manager in the organization
items.x: A change is the addition, modification or removal of anything that could have a direct or indirect effect on services. Change enablement makes sure the risks of changes are properly assessed.

items.q: What is a workaround?
o: A solution that reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem for which a full resolution is not yet available
A permanent fix for a problem
A change implemented without authorization
A way of avoiding the service desk
items.x: A workaround reduces or eliminates the impact of an incident or problem while no full resolution is available. Some workarounds also reduce the likelihood of incidents.

items.q: What is an event?
o: A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents
Any change of state that has significance for the management of a service or other configuration item
A scheduled meeting with the customer
An unplanned interruption to a service
items.x: An event is any change of state that has significance for managing a service or configuration item. Events can be informational, warnings or exceptions, and only some lead to incidents.

items.q: A provider meets every SLA target each month, but users are frustrated and the customer is considering another provider. What is this situation commonly called?
o: The service relationship model
Value co-creation
A known error
The watermelon effect
items.x: The watermelon effect describes reports that are green on the outside, with every target met, while the experience is red on the inside. It happens when agreements measure technical outputs instead of the outcomes and experience users care about.

items.q: An organization uses a service integrator to coordinate many suppliers so that they work together as one ecosystem. What is this approach called?
o: Service integration and management (SIAM)
Value stream mapping
Business relationship management
Portfolio management
items.x: SIAM is an approach for managing multiple suppliers in an integrated way, often through a service integrator. It relates to the partners and suppliers dimension.

items.q: Which of the following is MOST closely associated with the value streams and processes dimension?
o: Contracts with suppliers
The culture of the organization
Defining the activities, workflows, controls and procedures needed to create value
The technologies used to store information
items.x: Value streams and processes define how work is done: activities, workflows, controls and procedures, and how they combine to create value. Contracts belong to partners and suppliers, culture to organizations and people, and technology to information and technology.

items.q: New regulations require data centres to report and reduce their energy consumption. Under PESTLE, which type of external factor is MOST directly involved?
o: Social
Economic
Political
Environmental
items.x: Energy use and carbon impact are Environmental factors. They are increasingly important for sustainability in product and service management.

items.q: Staff worry that new AI tools will replace them. Leaders explain how roles will change and provide training in new skills. Which dimension is MOST directly being addressed?
o: Information and technology
Organizations and people
Partners and suppliers
Value streams and processes
items.x: Culture, roles, competencies, training and how people adapt to change, including AI, all belong to the organizations and people dimension.

items.q: A team turns validated customer needs into specifications, an architecture and a clickable prototype, considering usability, supportability and sustainability. Which lifecycle activity is this?
o: Discover
Design
Build
Deliver
items.x: Design translates validated needs into specifications, architectures and prototypes. Good design considers experience, usability, supportability and sustainability as well as functionality.

items.q: A tested release is moved into the live environment, and the arrangements with a new hosting supplier are put into effect. Which lifecycle activity is this?
o: Build
Acquire
Operate
Transition
items.x: Transition moves new or changed products and services into the live environment, including the related arrangements such as onboarding or offboarding suppliers.

items.q: A new collaboration tool is ready. The team onboards employees, gives them access and makes sure they can actually use the service. Which lifecycle activity is this?
o: Deliver
Discover
Acquire
Build
items.x: Deliver makes products and services available and usable for consumers and users, including onboarding and access. Operate keeps the product running, and Support helps and restores when things go wrong.

items.q: Which statement about product versions and the product and service lifecycle is CORRECT?
o: A product must finish Support before a new version can enter Design
Only one lifecycle activity can be performed by an organization at a time
Different versions of the same product can be in different lifecycle activities at the same time
The lifecycle applies only to products built in-house
items.x: The lifecycle is non-linear. While version 2 is being operated and supported, version 3 can be in design or build. The lifecycle also applies to products that are acquired from suppliers rather than built.

items.q: Which is a recommendation for applying the 'focus on value' principle?
o: Encourage a focus on value among all staff, not only those who deal directly with customers
Measure only the costs of each service
Focus on value only during improvement projects
Let the service provider decide what consumers value
items.x: Recommendations for applying 'focus on value' include: know how consumers use each service, encourage a focus on value among all staff, focus on value during normal operations as well as improvements, and include value in every step of improvement initiatives.

items.q: After a careful assessment, a team concludes that its old processes are so poor that none of them can be kept. Which statement reflects ITIL guidance for 'start where you are'?
o: The team must still reuse at least half of the existing processes
The team should stop the initiative
The team should never assess the current state
It is acceptable: sometimes nothing from the current state can be reused
items.x: 'Start where you are' encourages reusing what works, but also recognizes that sometimes nothing from the current state can be reused. The decision must be based on objective assessment and risk management.

items.q: A manager says: 'Our iterations must be quick, so each one can deliver half-finished work.' Which guidance from 'progress iteratively with feedback' does this contradict?
o: Collaboration does not mean consensus
Simplify before automating
Fast does not mean incomplete
Observe directly
items.x: Each iteration should deliver something usable, even if it is small, such as a minimum viable product. Speed should never mean delivering incomplete, unusable results.

items.q: 'Decisions can only be made on visible data' is guidance for applying which guiding principle?
o: Focus on value
Collaborate and promote visibility
Start where you are
Keep it simple and practical
items.x: Collaborating and promoting visibility means making work, data and decisions transparent. Hidden information leads to poor decisions and resistance.

items.q: A team speeds up software releases but never tells the service desk about new features, and the desk is overwhelmed with calls. Which guiding principle was MOST clearly neglected?
o: Think and work holistically
Start where you are
Optimize and automate
Keep it simple and practical
items.x: Changing one part of the system without considering the others, such as support, knowledge and user communication, causes problems elsewhere. 'Think and work holistically' asks teams to manage the product or service as a whole.

items.q: A team tries to design a process that handles every possible exception, and the process becomes very complicated. What does 'keep it simple and practical' recommend?
o: Add more approval steps to control the exceptions
Stop using processes
Design rules that can handle exceptions generally, instead of a solution for every exception
Automate the complicated process as it is
items.x: Trying to provide a solution for every exception often leads to over-complication. 'Keep it simple and practical' recommends general rules for exceptions and the minimum number of steps.

items.q: Which statement is part of the 'optimize and automate' principle?
o: Every manual activity must be automated immediately
Automation should replace all people involved in a process
Optimization means making something perfect before it is used
Human intervention should only happen where it really contributes value
items.x: Resources, especially people, should be used to best effect. Technology should do what it is capable of, and humans should intervene where they really add value. Optimization means making something as effective and useful as it needs to be, not perfect.

items.q: Which governance activity checks the performance of the organization, its practices, products and services, and their conformance with policies and direction?
o: Evaluate
Monitor
Direct
Deliver
items.x: 'Monitor' checks performance and conformance. 'Evaluate' considers the organization, strategy and environment, and 'direct' sets strategies and policies.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of GOVERNANCE rather than management?
o: The board sets the organization's risk appetite and policy for the use of AI
A team leader allocates incidents to analysts
A project manager updates a project plan
A service desk agent resets a password
items.x: Governance is about direction and control at the highest level: evaluating, setting strategy and policy (direct), and monitoring. Assigning work and running activities within that direction is management.

items.q: In which step of the continual improvement model is the improvement plan defined, for example as a series of iterations?
o: Where are we now?
Did we get there?
How do we get there?
What is the vision?
items.x: 'How do we get there?' defines the plan to close the gap between the current state and the target state. This may be a single initiative or a series of iterations.

items.q: What is typically done in the step 'How do we keep the momentum going?'
o: The baseline assessment is performed
The improvement plan is first defined
The vision is agreed
The change is embedded, successes are recognized and the next improvements are identified
items.x: The final step sustains the improvement. It embeds new ways of working, communicates and celebrates success, captures lessons and feeds new opportunities back into the cycle.

items.q: How many improvement methods does ITIL recommend that an organization uses?
o: As many as possible, to cover every situation
A small number of key methods that suit the organization and the types of improvement it handles
Only one method for every situation
Only the methods required by regulators
items.x: Using too many methods causes confusion. ITIL recommends selecting a few key methods, for example Lean, Agile techniques or SWOT, that suit the organization, and using them consistently.

items.q: How many management practices are described in ITIL (Version 5)?
items.x: ITIL (Version 5) keeps the 34 management practices, reorganized into two groups: general management and product and service management. 26 is the number of ITIL v3 processes.

items.q: What is the purpose of the change enablement practice?
o: To make new and changed features available for use
To move components into live environments
To maximize the number of successful product and service changes by ensuring that risks have been properly assessed, authorizing changes to proceed, and managing the change schedule
To manage the people side of organizational change
items.x: Change enablement balances beneficial change against protection from adverse effects. Option A is release management, option B deployment management, and option D organizational change management.

items.q: In the ITIL value system, what is meant by 'opportunity'?
o: The need or desire for products and services among consumers
Options or possibilities to add value for stakeholders or otherwise improve the organization
A risk that has been accepted
A request for change
items.x: Opportunity represents options or possibilities to add value or improve the organization. Option A describes demand. Both are inputs that trigger activities in the value system.

items.q: What is the outcome of the ITIL value system?
o: Products
Incidents
Practices
Value
items.x: The value system turns opportunity and demand into value for the organization, its customers and other stakeholders, through products and services.

items.q: When mapping a value stream for improvement, what is normally mapped FIRST?
o: The current (as-is) state of the value stream
The ideal future state, ignoring the current situation
The organization chart
The list of software tools in use
items.x: Value stream mapping usually starts with the current state, so that waste and bottlenecks become visible. The future (to-be) state and improvement plan are then designed. This reflects 'start where you are'.

items.q: Which of the following is a typical example of waste found when mapping a value stream?
o: Testing a release before deployment
Gathering requirements from customers
Work waiting several days in a queue for an approval that adds little value
Delivering the product to the consumer
items.x: Waiting, unnecessary hand-offs, rework and approvals that add no value are common forms of waste. Mapping makes them visible so that the flow can be improved.

items.q: What is the main purpose of AI governance?
o: To replace management decision-making with AI
To make sure AI is used responsibly, ethically and in line with the organization's policies, risk appetite and legal obligations, with clear accountability and oversight
To buy the most advanced AI tools available
To prevent the organization from using any AI
items.x: AI governance applies evaluate, direct and monitor to AI. It sets policies, defines accountability, manages risks such as bias, errors and privacy, and makes sure human oversight is appropriate.

items.q: Which statement BEST describes Lean in relation to ITIL?
o: Lean is a certification for organizations
Lean replaces the four dimensions
Lean is a software development language
Lean focuses on maximizing value by eliminating waste and improving flow, and supports techniques such as value stream mapping used with ITIL
items.x: Lean thinking, which originated in manufacturing, focuses on value, flow and waste reduction. ITIL builds on Lean ideas, for example in value stream mapping and in the principle 'keep it simple and practical'.
